line 13: Giving talks in spaces like this brings me back to the same principle, time and time again:
line 14: Art belongs to everyone.
line 17: Michael Burgess, a creative producer working across culture put it plainly: “yes, we want to sell art, but I want to make sure there is meaning, purpose and consciousness in this function.” As new audiences enter the art world, the question goes beyond where we put the work. How do we make people feel that the conversation belongs to them, too?
line 18: Ulrich Schrauth, curator and creative director, came at it from a different angle. Museums come to him and say “we want to diversify our audiences, can we do something digital” and his answer is always the same. “You have to think from the ground up how to represent these voices and how to interweave them.”
line 19: So what do cultural spaces need for the next generation? Collaboration, for one. Places where people can gather, make memories and feel safe enough to speak. They also need urgency. We’re living through disruptive times, and art should make room for political conversation and action, not just reflect on them years later.
line 20: And they need stories. Whose roots shaped the work? Who was it made for? How did it arrive in this room? Those questions can give someone a way in, especially when the language around art makes them feel they need permission to speak.
line 22: W1 saw that gallery spaces weren’t keeping up with how people experience art, and they built the tech before anyone else was thinking that way. Nobody took them seriously at first, but now their screens are built for purpose. So if galleries are struggling, the real question isn’t digital versus physical, it’s how do you support artists in a way that uses both?
line 23: This makes me hopeful. Not that the barriers and gatekeepers to the art world don’t exist. Trust me, they do. Money, gender, race, location: there are many ways to be kept outside. But these new spaces open a different door.
line 24: Someone who would never plan a gallery visit might find themselves standing inside a painting on a night out. My great swathes of colour, which usually live quietly on a single canvas, suddenly surrounded the room. The work hadn’t changed, but its invitation had.
